name: boat-anchor
intent: Records what a Boat Anchor costs: code, configuration or a dependency that is kept in the system although nothing uses it — and the price is the reader's time, the compiler's and linker's work, the security surface, and the false certainty that the thing is load-bearing when it is not.
problem: Something is retained on the belief it will be needed later, or because nobody could prove it was safe to remove. The belief is usually wrong, and it is expensive in a way that is invisible: the code compiles, passes review, and never runs.
context: The extension of the term from obsolete hardware to software names an anti-pattern of unused source code or other components left in a codebase, introducing unnecessary complexity and maintenance. The consequences named are specific: boat anchors exacerbate memory usage, file size and compile times, and they add security risk, because unused dependencies are not scanned or patched with the same attention as used ones. The subtlety, and the reason the name is apt, is the epistemic problem rather than the physical one — there is no evidence in the code of whether a component is used, so determining it requires asking a person, which is slow and which people get wrong. Wikipedia notes the failure mode that code kept 'just in case' can be accidentally restored to live by a later linking change. The remedy is deletion; if it must be retained, isolate it so the compiler excludes it, and rely on version control rather than commented-out source, which is the opposite of what it is usually used for.
benefits: Reader time returns: dead code is noise a reader must classify before they can read the live code, and classification requires knowledge the code does not carry.
The compiler does less work and the build gets faster — link time and binary size shrink measurably when unused translation units and libraries are dropped.
The security surface shrinks: an unused dependency is one that is often out of date, unpatched, and outside the team's working familiarity, and it is reachable by any future code that imports it.
The dependency graph stops lying: the manifest describes what the system needs rather than what it once considered.
Uncertainty goes away. The question 'is this used?' is the expensive part, and deleting converts an unanswerable question into a fact.
tradeoffs: Removing it requires evidence, and evidence can be hard to obtain in a system with reflection, dynamic loading or registration by string name — where a call site exists that no static tool can find. The 30-50% unowned-code figure reported for a research-originated system in the AntiPatterns account of Lava Flow is the extreme of this.
Version control does not make deletion free: it makes the *code* recoverable, not the *knowledge* — the reason it was kept, and whether the condition that required it can recur.

The removal is not always a deletion. Sometimes the code is dead but its configuration, schema entry, feature flag or dependency declaration is still loaded at runtime, and the cleanup has to remove all of them together.

A genuinely speculative component has a real, if small, value: if the situation it exists for arrives within its lifetime, writing it then costs less than reading it now. The judgement is about expected value, and it is frequently made wrongly in both directions.

The cost is sometimes social rather than technical. A component that a specific person owns or that a departing colleague left behind can be politically expensive to remove even when it is clearly dead.

Deleting commented-out code is sometimes a loss: in a system where version control is unreliable (a legacy VCS, an exported tarball with no history), commented-out code can be the only copy of something.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Reliability and scalability stay high because dead code is not executed — the harm is entirely indirect. Security is the one runtime-relevant axis that suffers, and it suffers for a specific reason: an unused, unpinned or unpatched dependency is still something a future import (or a transitive resolution) can bring into the live path. Discoverability is the axis that actually defines the smell: nothing in the code says whether a component is used.

participants.responsibility: The retained component: a class, module, dependency, configuration block, schema migration or commented-out block that no live path reaches.
participants.notes: The defining property is not that it is obsolete but that nothing in the code demonstrates whether it is used.

participants.responsibility: The developer or organisation keeping it — on the belief it will be needed, because the cost of proving removal safe is unknown, or because ownership is unclear.
participants.notes: The retention decision is usually made once, by someone who has left.

participants.responsibility: Anyone working in the codebase, who must classify each component as live or dead before they can read it.
participants.notes: Without that classification the reader either trusts everything or audits everything.

use_cases: Classes or whole sections that still exist, still compile, and are never referenced within their codebase — the case described in the daily anti-pattern account, where nobody could tell whether they were used without asking someone.
Commented-out code blocks kept 'for later', when version control already holds them — which is exactly the use version control exists for.
TODO comments inside functions that were never actioned, so the reader spends time on a promise that was never kept.
Dependencies in a manifest no module imports, including transitive ones pulled in by a direct dependency that no longer needs them.
Obsolete documentation and docstrings that now describe behaviour the code no longer has, making the documentation actively misleading.
Feature flags, configuration keys and schema columns for a feature that was removed and whose cleanup was never done.
Build-system sections that emit code or assets no longer referenced — the game-engine example of dropping the 3D pipeline from a 2D build.
avoid_when: Version control is unreliable or unavailable (a vendored tarball, a legacy VCS, an offline environment) — in that case a copy outside the build tree is a genuine backup, though it must not be compiled.
The code is the only specification of a behaviour that must be preserved — for a system with no tests and no history, deleting the last copy of an algorithm is a real risk.
It is genuinely reachable through reflection, dynamic loading, plugin registration by string, or a configuration table, in which case it is live code that static analysis cannot see.
The component is a licence or compliance obligation (an attribution file, a bundled licence text, an SBOM entry) rather than code.
The removal is not verifiable: if you cannot demonstrate that nothing reaches it, you have not found a boat anchor, you have found code you cannot analyse.
It is under active development with a named owner and a dated plan; that is speculation with a schedule, which is a different thing.
pitfalls: Commenting code out instead of deleting it: this keeps the noise, still gets read, still gets flagged by linters, and is not a backup as long as version control exists.
Deleting the code but leaving the dependency, the configuration key or the schema entry, so the system still carries the weight and still fails to explain itself.
Trusting a static analyser blindly in reflective or plugin-based systems, and either deleting live code or keeping dead code based on a report that could not see the dynamic paths.
Removing code that is dormant but load-bearing for a rare failure path, and finding out during an incident that the 'unused' branch was the recovery path.
Generalising from the first deletion: 'unused' often means 'used by one caller far away', so a first pass should look for a single owner before removing.
Leaving a stub that logs a deprecation warning forever. The warning is a contract you will keep honouring; a versioned removal date is a commitment with an end.

related_patterns_notes.feature-toggle: A feature toggle is the legitimate form of 'keep it, it may be used later' — the code is live and the *path* to it is data. The boat anchor is the same belief applied to something no flag can switch on.
related_patterns_notes.module: Modules are the unit a boat anchor lives in and the granularity at which a build system can exclude it, which is the mitigation the pattern description names: isolate so the compiler leaves it out.
related_patterns_notes.registry: Registration by string name is the mechanism that makes boat anchors undetectable: a registry keeps a reference so a later lookup can succeed, which converts dead code into live code by definition and defeats the analysis.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: A plugin discovered at runtime is the honest counterpart of the problem: it is why some components cannot be proven dead, and the reason a plugin's liveness must be asserted by its own registration test.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-initialization: Lazy initialisation is a cost, not a boat anchor: the code runs, so it is not dead. The confusing overlap is that both are invisible until exercised.
related_patterns_notes.version-number: A version number is the mechanism for the removal plan that makes an anchor temporary: 'used if 2.0' is a boat anchor with an expiry, and without one it is just an anchor.

anti_patterns: The 'just in case' class: kept because a related feature was once planned, with no name, no owner and no date attached to the belief.
Commented-out code blocks — the canonical boat anchor and a misuse of the practice version control already does better.
TODO comments left in place across several releases, so the codebase's stated intentions never shrink.
Dependencies in the manifest that no module imports, kept because removing them requires editing a lockfile and someone worried about the transitive tree.
Obsolete docstrings and wiki pages describing behaviour that no longer exists, so the documentation is worse than nothing.
Configuration keys, feature flags and schema columns left behind after a feature was removed, still loaded at startup and still validated.
Build outputs and vendored assets for platforms or features that are no longer shipped.
The 'I could not prove it was unused' retention: when the cost of analysis exceeds the cost of keeping, nothing is ever removed, and the accumulation is permanent.
design_principles: You ain't gonna need it (YAGNI): code for a hypothetical future requirement costs a reader today and buys nothing unless the requirement arrives.
Delete rather than disable: a disabled path is still a path someone must reason about; a deleted one is gone from the graph.
Version control is the archive: history, not commented-out source, is the mechanism for retrieving something that was removed.
Make liveness observable: a component that is genuinely live should be reachable from a documented entry point; one that is not should be removable without an argument.
Prefer the gate to the guess: a version check, a deadline or an owner turns 'keep it in case' into a decision with a date attached.
best_practices: Run unused-code detection in CI as a ratchet: accept the current report once, then fail on any increase, so the count can only go down.

Require evidence before deleting: a reference search across the whole tree, a build that succeeds, and a test run that covers the surrounding area. If any is missing, you have not proved it is an anchor.
Exclude at the build level rather than commenting out: move it out of the compilation set or behind a build flag, so it is neither read nor linked nor shipped.
Audit dependencies separately from source: unused direct dependencies are invisible to code review, and they are the highest-severity instances because they carry their own CVE surface.
Remove the residue too — dependency, config key, flag, migration, test fixture and doc — in the same commit as the code, or the anchor is only half raised.
Attach an expiry to anything retained: a version number, a date, or a named condition. A retention without one is an accident that will be permanent.

Treat 'I could not prove it unused' as a finding about the codebase's analysability, not as a reason to keep the code: it usually points at reflection, string-based registration or an unclear ownership boundary.
Use review as the sunlight: a reviewer who asks 'what calls this?' removes anchors cheaply, because the person who wrote it is usually not the person reviewing it.
sources: The term 'boat anchor' transferred from obsolete radio equipment and computers to relic software; Wikipedia records the software usage as unused source code or components left in a codebase, with the costs named as memory, file size, compile time and security risk.
YAGNI ('You Aren't Gonna Need It'), the oldest of the programming adages cited as the remedy in the daily anti-pattern account of boat anchors.

The same account records the honest counter-example: in more than half of the affected projects, code that was removed had to be added back later — which is why the decision needs evidence rather than doctrine.
